Background/Diffusion-Language-Models.title: Diffusion Language Models
Background/Diffusion-Language-Models.content:
overview

A diffusion language model generates a whole text at once, by starting from noise and
denoising every position in parallel, instead of writing it left to right. The variants differ
in where the noise lives: on continuous embeddings of the tokens, or on the tokens themselves
(replaced by random tokens, or masked). Masked diffusion is the variant that now scales. This
note is a map of the variants and of what each offers the relational models of this vault.


Sources: Austin et al., Structured Denoising Diffusion Models in Discrete State-Spaces (D3PM), NeurIPS 2021; Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation, NeurIPS 2022; Dieleman et al., Continuous Diffusion for Categorical Data (CDCD), 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, Likelihood-Based Diffusion Language Models (Plaid), 2023; Lou, Meng & Ermon, Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution (SEDD), ICML 2024; Sahoo et al., Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLM), NeurIPS 2024; Shi et al., Simplified and Generalized Masked Diffusion for Discrete Data (MD4), 2024; Nie et al., Large Language Diffusion Models (LLaDA), 2025; Arriola et al., Block Diffusion (BD3-LM), 2025. An overview written from these papers; nothing here is measured in this repository.
Bibliography: Austin et al. 2021 · Li et al. 2022 · Dieleman et al. 2022 · Gulrajani & Hashimoto 2023 · Lou et al. 2024 · Sahoo et al. 2024 · Shi et al. 2024 · Nie et al. 2025 · Arriola et al. 2025
Lenticulum (vault): Language Models · Implicit Diffusion Learners

1. The idea
An autoregressive model factorises p(x_1, \dots, x_L) = \prod_i p(x_i \mid x_{<i}) and generates one token at a time.
A diffusion model instead defines a forward process that corrupts a text step by step until
nothing is left, and learns the reverse process: given a corrupted text and the noise level,
predict the clean one. Generation runs the reverse process from pure noise. Every position is
updated at every step, so the model sees the whole text in both directions. Infilling, editing
and constraints on any position are then natural, not special cases. How a Diffusion Language
Model Generates goes through the steps.
2. The variants









































familythe noisy statethe network predictsexamplescontinuous, on embeddingseach token’s embedding plus Gaussian noisethe clean embedding (or the noise), then a rounding step to tokensDiffusion-LM, CDCD, Plaiddiscrete, uniformeach token replaced, with growing probability, by a random tokenthe distribution of the clean token at each positionD3PM (uniform transitions)discrete, absorbing (masked)each token replaced, with growing probability, by a [MASK] tokenthe clean token at each masked positionD3PM (absorbing), MDLM, MD4, LLaDAdiscrete, score-basedas above (uniform or absorbing)ratios p(y)/p(x) of neighbouring sequences, the discrete analogue of the scoreSEDDblock (semi-autoregressive)blocks generated left to right, masked diffusion within a blockas for masked diffusion, conditioned on the earlier blocksBD3-LM

Continuous. Diffusion-LM diffuses in a learned embedding space, and its gradient guidance
gives controllable generation (syntax, length, content). Its embeddings are learned together
with the denoiser, which needs care: Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model.

CDCD trains the denoiser with a cross-entropy loss over the vocabulary and normalises the
embeddings (“score interpolation”, “time warping”).
Plaid studies the likelihood scaling of continuous models.


Masked. The forward process masks each token independently. MDLM and MD4 showed that the
training objective simplifies to a weighted mixture of masked-language-modelling losses (as in
BERT), one per masking rate. That made masked diffusion simple to train and competitive with
autoregressive models of the same size. LLaDA trained such a model at the 8-billion-parameter
scale.
Score-based discrete. SEDD learns the ratios of the data distribution between sequences
that differ in one token. That is the “score” of a discrete distribution, and the paper reports
perplexities competitive with autoregressive models of GPT-2’s size.
Block. BD3-LM interpolates between the two worlds: autoregressive over blocks, diffusion
within a block. That brings back variable-length generation and key-value caching.

3. What they offer this vault

Every query direction. A diffusion model conditions on any set of positions and fills the
rest. That is the clamp-and-solve interface of Lenticulum’s implicit learners
(tokens: queries as clamps).
A relation, not only a sampler. The denoiser at small noise points towards the data. Its
fixed points or stable roots are the texts the model “accepts”. That is the sense in which a
model is a relation over text (Meaning as a Relation over Text).
The choice ahead (Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners §3): Lenticulum’s
learners are continuous (roots, Laplace weights, adjoints), which is the Diffusion-LM family,
while the masked discrete family is the one that scales. A discrete implicit learner would join
them.

Related: How a Diffusion Language Model Generates, Meaning as a Relation over Text,
Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model, Factor Graphs against Mixtures of Experts and Agent Chains

Background/Embeddings-in-a-Diffusion-Lan.filePath: Background/Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model.md
Background/Embeddings-in-a-Diffusion-Lan.title: Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model
Background/Embeddings-in-a-Diffusion-Lan.content:
design

A language model usually works on embeddings: each token becomes a learned vector. For a
diffusion model on continuous embeddings, learned embeddings are a known source of trouble:
trained with the denoiser, they can collapse to make denoising trivial, so they are normalised
or anchored. A factor graph whose variables each had their own, drifting embedding would make it
worse, since messages between variables need one code. Discrete diffusion works without an
embedding in its state, and there is precedent for models without a token embedding at all.


Sources: Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation, NeurIPS 2022; Dieleman et al., Continuous Diffusion for Categorical Data (CDCD), 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, Likelihood-Based Diffusion Language Models (Plaid), 2023; Sahoo et al. (MDLM), NeurIPS 2024; Xue et al., ByT5, 2021; Yu et al., MEGABYTE, 2023; Pagnoni et al., Byte Latent Transformer, 2024. The collapse argument (§2) is an interpretation in Lenticulum’s terms, not measured here. code: tokens.jl
Bibliography: Li et al. 2022 · Dieleman et al. 2022 · Gulrajani & Hashimoto 2023 · Xue et al. 2021 · Yu et al. 2023 · Pagnoni et al. 2024
Lenticulum (vault): Why Learned Relations Do Not Collapse · Language Models

1. Where embeddings enter

In the network. Every model embeds tokens at its input and maps back to the vocabulary at its
output. That is internal to the network and harmless: it is how the denoiser computes.
In the diffusion state. Only continuous diffusion (Diffusion-LM, CDCD, Plaid) puts embeddings
in the noisy state itself: the state is a matrix of embedding vectors plus noise. Discrete
diffusion (D3PM, MDLM, SEDD, LLaDA) noises the tokens: its state is a sequence of tokens and
masks, with no embedding.
In this repository. tokens codes each token as a one-hot block, a fixed code with no
learned embedding in the state. That is the simplest embedding-free choice, at a dimension equal
to the vocabulary size.

2. Learned embeddings in the state: the collapse problem
If the embeddings are learned together with the denoiser, the objective can be lowered by moving
them instead of by denoising better. Shrinking all embeddings towards each other makes the noise
relatively large, and the problem changes. Pushing them far apart makes the noisy states trivially
separable. Diffusion-LM trains the embeddings jointly and adds a rounding term that ties
the clean state to a token. CDCD normalises the embeddings and trains with a cross-entropy over
tokens. Both are ways of fixing the scale the objective would otherwise exploit.
In Lenticulum’s terms this is the collapse of a learned relation whose coordinates are not fixed:
the embedding is a learned change of variables. Without its Jacobian (or a fixed normalisation) the
objective can be satisfied by squashing or stretching the space instead of by fitting.
Why Learned Relations Do Not Collapse
goes through the same mechanism for other factors. The cure has the same shape: fix the scale
(normalised or anchored embeddings), or pay for it (a log-Jacobian).
3. One embedding per variable?
The question: in a factor graph of such models, if every variable had its own embedding and the
embeddings drifted as the parts were learned, would that be a problem? Yes, for three reasons.

Messages need a common code. A message from one factor to a variable is a belief over that
variable’s values. If two factors on the same variable use different embeddings, their messages
live in different spaces, and the product of the beliefs is undefined until a map between the
codes is fixed. That map is either learned too, which is one more drifting part, or the
embedding is shared.
Drift breaks composition. A factor learned against one embedding is wrong once the embedding
moves. Relations composed by product assume their coordinates mean the same thing on both
sides of every shared variable.
Collapse, per variable. Each learned embedding is a place where §2’s collapse can happen.

So embeddings should be shared and fixed across the graph, or learned once and frozen before the
parts are, or replaced by a discrete code.
4. Embedding-free, and the precedent

Discrete state, internal embeddings. Masked diffusion has no embedding in its state.
Variables are tokens, and messages are categorical beliefs over the vocabulary, which pool
exactly. This is what Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners §3 means by
per-position categorical beliefs. The networks still embed internally, but nothing drifts
between factors.
Byte-level models. ByT5 works on bytes, with no learned tokeniser and a vocabulary of 256.
MEGABYTE and the Byte Latent Transformer group bytes into patches, the latter of dynamic size, and
report scaling competitive with token models. The state is the raw bytes; any embedding is inside
the network.
One-hot codes, as here: exact and fixed, but of the vocabulary’s dimension. They are practical
for characters or bytes, and too wide for a 50 000-token vocabulary in a continuous state.

A suggestion, not tested: variables as tokens or bytes with categorical beliefs (discrete,
embedding-free), embeddings only inside each factor’s network, and latent summary variables (the
long-range structure of §3 there) in a code that is learned once and then fixed.
Related: Diffusion Language Models, Meaning as a Relation over Text, tokens

Background/Factor-Graphs-against-Mixture.filePath: Background/Factor Graphs against Mixtures of Experts and Agent Chains.md
Background/Factor-Graphs-against-Mixture.title: Factor Graphs against Mixtures of Experts and Agent Chains
Background/Factor-Graphs-against-Mixture.content:
comparison

A mixture of experts routes each input to a few sub-networks and mixes their outputs; an agent
chain passes a text from one model or tool to the next. Both pass points forward: one routing
decision, one intermediate text. A factor graph with a belief algebra passes beliefs in every
direction. Several hypotheses survive until evidence decides between them, a constraint added
later can correct an earlier step, and the whole is scored by one free energy. This note says what
that buys and what it costs.


Sources: Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan & Hinton, Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts, Neural Computation 1991; Shazeer et al., Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer, 2017; Fedus, Zoph & Shazeer, Switch Transformers, 2021; Hinton, Training Products of Experts by Minimizing Contrastive Divergence, Neural Computation 2002; Yao et al., ReAct, 2022. The comparison is original to this vault; nothing here is measured.
Bibliography: Jacobs et al. 1991 · Shazeer et al. 2017 · Fedus et al. 2021 · Hinton 2002 · Yao et al. 2022
Lenticulum (vault): Belief Algebra · Messages are Inversions · Switching Constraint Factors · RQ-008 Overlays, Mixtures and Tropical Limits

1. Three ways to combine models









































mixture of expertsagent chainfactor graph with beliefswhat flowsan input to the chosen experts, their weighted outputsone text (or tool result) per stepa belief per variable (a distribution), in every directioncombinationa sum of experts, gated by the inputcomposition of steps, in ordera product of factors, inferred jointlydecisionsrouting per token (top-1, top-2)each step commits to its outputcommitted only when the beliefs are sharpcorrectionnone after routinga later step can only reacta later factor’s evidence flows back to earlier variablesa global scorethe training lossnone (each step’s own)the free energy of the whole graph
2. A mixture of experts is a switch; a product of experts is an overlay

A mixture of experts (Jacobs et al. 1991) is p(y \mid x) = \sum_k g_k(x)\, p_k(y \mid x): a gate picks experts and
their predictions are averaged. In a factor graph that is a switching factor: a discrete
outcome k with the gate’s weights, and per outcome its expert. The sparse layers of large
networks (Shazeer et al. 2017, Switch Transformers) keep only the top one or two outcomes, a hard
switch that is cheap to compute. The graph keeps the outcome’s posterior instead. Evidence
downstream can then revise which expert applied.
A product of experts (Hinton 2002) is \prod_k p_k(y)/Z: every expert must agree, and each vetoes
what it rejects. In a factor graph that is an overlay of factors on the same variables.
Lenticulum’s OverlayFactor implements it, and with normalisation in the data channels it is a
product of Gaussian experts or a mixture of experts. A product sharpens, and a sum broadens.
Overlaying convex energies cannot create several modes; the switch can. A switch is exactly a
linear constraint overlaid with a concave piecewise-linear term (Lenticulum’s RQ-008).

3. An agent chain is a composition of point maps
An agent chain (ReAct and its successors) alternates a model’s reasoning with tool calls. Each step
reads the previous step’s text and writes the next. In Lenticulum’s terms every step is a point
lens: its output is a Dirac belief, one committed text, and it runs in one direction.
Uncertainty does not propagate. If step 2 was unsure between two readings, step 3 sees only the
one that was written down. A later failure cannot correct step 2 except by rerunning the chain, which is
what retries and reflection prompts do by hand.
4. What the belief algebra buys
With beliefs on the variables (categorical over tokens or options, Gaussian over latent
coordinates, mixtures for several hypotheses):

Several hypotheses stay alive. A mixture belief carries both readings until evidence decides.
Messages run both ways. A constraint on the answer (a checker, a type, a unit test, a
required format) sends a message back to the variables it depends on and reweights them. That is
verification inside inference, not after it.
Additions are factors. A new requirement is a factor added to the product. Its effect on every
other variable follows from inference, with no new routing logic.
One score. The free energy is comparable across structures. That is what lets Lenticulum
search over graph structures by it (structure edits, cluster nodes).

5. What it costs

Inference is not free. Exact inference is exponential in the discrete variables a cluster
joins; belief propagation on loops is approximate; mixtures grow with every switch unless reduced.
A chain of point maps is cheap because it decides early.
Beliefs over text are hard. A distribution over whole texts has no closed form. In practice
beliefs are per position (categorical over the vocabulary) or over latent summaries, and the
dependencies between positions must come from factors, or they are lost.
Learning has to be designed. Each part must be a normalised density in its data channels or
trained by comparison, or it collapses
(Why Learned Relations Do Not Collapse),
and naive joint training of many parts is not expected to converge easily. Distilling the parts
from a large model, subgraph by subgraph, is the route this repository plans
(Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners §3, the moonshot).

6. A sketch
A question-answering system as a factor graph:

Variables: the question (clamped), a latent reading of it (categorical over interpretations),
retrieved facts (categorical over candidates), an answer (tokens).
Factors:

a parser relating the question to readings;
a retriever relating readings to facts;
a generator relating readings and facts to the answer;
a checker on the answer, for format or consistency with the facts.



Inference returns beliefs over readings and answers together. A checker that rejects an answer
lowers the weight of the reading that produced it. An agent chain would have committed to one
reading at the first step.
Related: Diffusion Language Models, Meaning as a Relation over Text,
Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model

Background/How-a-Diffusion-Language-Mode.filePath: Background/How a Diffusion Language Model Generates.md
Background/How-a-Diffusion-Language-Mode.title: How a Diffusion Language Model Generates
Background/How-a-Diffusion-Language-Mode.content:
algorithm

Generation runs the corruption backwards: start from a fully masked (or fully noisy) text, and at
each step let the network predict every position, then commit some of the predictions and
re-corrupt the rest. The number of steps trades speed against quality, and which predictions are
committed is a design choice of its own. Conditioning and infilling are clamps: the given tokens
are never corrupted.


Sources: Sahoo et al., Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLM), NeurIPS 2024; Nie et al., Large Language Diffusion Models (LLaDA), 2025; Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation, NeurIPS 2022; Lou, Meng & Ermon (SEDD), ICML 2024; Arriola et al., Block Diffusion, 2025. A summary of their samplers; nothing here is measured in this repository.
Bibliography: Sahoo et al. 2024 · Nie et al. 2025 · Li et al. 2022 · Arriola et al. 2025
Lenticulum (vault): Implicit Diffusion Learners

1. Masked diffusion, step by step
The forward process masks each token independently with probability t, the noise level from
0 (the text) to 1 (all masked). The network \hat p_\theta(x_i \mid z_t) predicts a distribution over the
vocabulary at every masked position i, given the partly masked text z_t. To generate L tokens in T
steps:

Start with z_1 = [\mathrm{MASK}]^L (the prompt’s positions, if any, are filled and stay filled).
For t = 1, 1 - \tfrac1T, \dots, \tfrac1T:

predict every masked position, \hat x_i \sim \hat p_\theta(\cdot \mid z_t), or take the most likely token;
commit a fraction of them, the expected number going from t to t - \tfrac1T, and keep the rest
masked.


After T steps nothing is masked: that is the text.

Which predictions to commit. The plain reverse process commits a random subset, as the
forward process masked one. LLaDA’s low-confidence remasking instead commits the most
confident predictions and re-masks the least confident. That is a heuristic, and the paper reports
it works better than random remasking. Committed tokens are never revised in the basic sampler. Revising them (re-masking
a committed token) is possible and is a choice of sampler.
Steps and quality. With T = L steps one token is committed per step, like an autoregressive
model in a learned order. With fewer steps several tokens are committed at once, from predictions
that were made independently per position given z_t. Positions that depend strongly on each other
(the two words of a fixed expression) can then come out inconsistent. That is the price of
parallel decoding, and the reason quality drops as T falls.
2. Continuous diffusion
In Diffusion-LM the state is a matrix of embeddings plus Gaussian noise. Each step denoises it,
like an image diffusion model, and at the end every position is rounded to its nearest
token’s embedding. Guidance is a gradient on the continuous state: a classifier’s
\nabla \log p(c \mid x_t) added to the score steers the text towards an attribute c. Rounding is the
weak point, because a state between two embeddings commits to one of them only at the end.
3. Score-based and block samplers

SEDD steps a continuous-time Markov chain whose rates are the learned ratios. It updates
several positions per step (“\tau-leaping”) or one position exactly.
Block diffusion generates block after block, each by masked diffusion conditioned on the
blocks before. It can stop at any block boundary, which gives variable length, and it reuses
earlier blocks’ computation.

4. Conditioning as clamping
Any token given in advance is fixed and never masked: a prompt (a prefix), a suffix, scattered
words, or a template with slots. The model fills the rest. In the relational reading of this vault,
a query clamps the known positions and solves for the free ones
(tokens; Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners §1). A diffusion model is a
solver that answers every such query with one network. The difference from a relation is that it
samples one answer per run. A relation’s interface instead enumerates the stable answers
(Lenticulum’s implicit_roots) or their mixture.
Related: Diffusion Language Models, Meaning as a Relation over Text

Background/Meaning-as-a-Relation-over-Te.filePath: Background/Meaning as a Relation over Text.md
Background/Meaning-as-a-Relation-over-Te.title: Meaning as a Relation over Text
Background/Meaning-as-a-Relation-over-Te.content:
design

A meaning does not pick out one text; it picks out a set of texts that express it, and a text
can carry several meanings. So meaning is naturally a relation between texts and meanings, or
between texts and texts (paraphrase, entailment, translation), not a function. A relational model
answers in every direction (generate from a meaning, read a meaning off a text, check that two
texts agree) and composes by product. This note makes that precise enough to build on, and says
what it does not settle.


Sources: original to this vault (design and interpretation). It uses Lenticulum’s reading of implicit learners as relations; no claim here is measured.
Lenticulum (vault): Implicit Diffusion Learners · Composing Diffusion Factors · Why Learned Relations Do Not Collapse
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Markov Category · Bayesian Inversion

1. Relations, not functions
Write T for texts and M for meanings, whatever represents them: a logical form, a latent vector,
a label, another text. A semantic relation is a subset R \subseteq T \times M, or, with uncertainty, a joint
density p(t, m) whose high-density set is R.

Many texts per meaning: the paraphrases of m are the fibre \{t : (t, m) \in R\}.
Many meanings per text: ambiguity, \{m : (t, m) \in R\} with more than one element.
Relations between texts: paraphrase (t \sim t' when they share a meaning), translation (texts in
two languages), entailment (an order, not an equivalence), and question and answer.

A function T \to M (a classifier) or M \to T (a generator) is one direction of such a relation, and loses
the other. A language model conditioned on a prompt is one slice of it: texts given a prefix.
2. A diffusion model as a relation
A denoiser at small noise moves a corrupted text towards the texts the model finds plausible. Its
fixed points, the texts it leaves unchanged at small noise, are the texts the model accepts.
Clamping some positions and solving for the rest is a query of the relation:

fix a meaning’s tokens (a topic, a slot filler, a constraint) and solve for the text;
fix a text and solve for a meaning’s coordinates;
fix two texts’ shared slots and ask whether a joint solution exists.

The relation is the set of all such solutions, and the network is one way to answer queries
of it (How a Diffusion Language Model Generates §4).
Composition is a product. Two relations on overlapping variables combine by multiplying their
densities, which adds their energies. For example: a fluency relation on the text, a content
relation between the text and a meaning, a style relation between the text and a style label.
The text then has to satisfy all of them, and each part can be learned separately. That is what
Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners builds, and the product’s smoothing bias is
its main known cost (§3 there).
3. What this does and does not give

It gives a common interface. Generation, understanding, checking and editing are queries of
one object. A constraint added at query time is a factor added to the product, not a retraining.
It does not give the meanings. Which M to use is open. It could be latent coordinates
learned with the text, another text (meaning as paraphrase class), or a formal representation.
The relational view only says how T and M are tied once both are there.
A learned relation can be degenerate. A relation that accepts every text is trivially
consistent with any data. Lenticulum’s analysis of when learned relations collapse applies
unchanged: a part must be a normalised density in its data channels, or be trained by
comparison (denoising is a comparison against injected noise). See
Why Learned Relations Do Not Collapse.
Spurious answers. The stable roots of a smoothed relation include points off the data, and
near-by branches merge. Lenticulum measures this on small relations
(VariationalDiffusion’s examples/calibration.md). For text that would mean fluent-looking
non-solutions and lost rare readings.

Related: Diffusion Language Models, Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model,
Factor Graphs against Mixtures of Experts and Agent Chains

Design/Assembling-a-Language-Model-from-.title: Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners
Design/Assembling-a-Language-Model-from-.content:
design overview

The plan of this repository. A diffusion language model whose parts are implicit
learners: each part is a relation over a few token positions, the model is their product,
and every query (continue, predict backwards, fill in, satisfy a constraint) is root finding
with the known tokens clamped. The first step, an n-gram chain assembled from closed-form
relations, is exact. What follows from it, and what stands in the way, is laid out here.


Sources: original to this vault (design); builds on Hinton, Training Products of Experts by Minimizing Contrastive Divergence, Neural Computation 2002; Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation, NeurIPS 2022; Austin et al., Structured Denoising Diffusion Models in Discrete State-Spaces, NeurIPS 2021; Sahoo et al., Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLM); Lou, Meng & Ermon, Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution (SEDD); Nie et al., Large Language Diffusion Models (LLaDA); Du et al., Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: Compositional Generation using Energy-Based Diffusion Models and MCMC, ICML 2023; Liu, Li, Du, Tenenbaum & Torralba, Compositional Visual Generation with Composable Diffusion Models, ECCV 2022; code: tokens.jl, sequence.jl
Bibliography: Hinton 2002 · Li et al. 2022 · Austin et al. 2021 · Sahoo et al. 2024 · Lou et al. 2024 · Nie et al. 2025 · Liu et al. 2022
Lenticulum (vault): Language Models · Implicit Diffusion Learners · Composing Diffusion Factors · product · Categorical Belief · Universal Approximation for Implicit Diffusion Learners
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Markov Category · Bayesian Inversion · Variational Free Energy

1. What is being built
Diffusion language models (MDLM, SEDD, LLaDA) already refine a whole sequence at once and can
fill in any masked positions. What they are not is modular: the model is one network over
the whole sequence, trained once, and nothing can be added to it at query time except guidance.
Lenticulum’s implicit learners are relations, and relations compose by product
(Composing Diffusion Factors).
So a language model can be assembled: separately learned relations over windows, spans or
latent summaries, combined into one model whose queries are answered jointly. The pieces this
needs, and what Lenticulum provides for each:






























piecein this repositoryfrom Lenticulumtext as a joint spacetokens: one block of V coordinates per position, tokens as one-hot codesthe joint space and its polarity (precision vector)a relation on a windowsequence: window_relation, closed form for nowImplicitDiffusion with any noise predictor; energy networksthe model as a productsequence: sequence_relation, windows and separatorsProductRelation with coordinates and weightsa query’s answerstoken_marginals, position_beliefsimplicit_mixture (every stable root, Laplace weights), CategoricalBelief
2. The first step: an n-gram chain, exactly
A chain of windows of width n, joined by separators on the overlaps,
p(x_1, \dots, x_L) = \frac{\prod_k p_{\mathrm{win}}(x_k, \dots, x_{k+n-1})}{\prod_k p_{\mathrm{sep}}(x_{k+1}, \dots, x_{k+n-1})},
is an (n-1)-th order Markov chain when the windows are its n-gram marginals. With closed-form
window relations (Gaussian mixtures at the codes of the n-grams), one assembled bigram model
over three symbols answers the continuation, the backward prediction and the infilling to within
10^{-4} of the closed form, finding every completion as a separate answer (sequence §3).
This is the Lenticulum chain of product.md §4 with a vocabulary. It establishes that the
assembly is right, and that the answers of a relation, read per position, are the categorical
marginals a language model must produce. It does not yet learn anything.
3. The decisions ahead
Continuous codes or a discrete learner. Lenticulum’s learners are continuous: a score or
energy on \mathbb R^d, with tokens as points. That is Diffusion-LM’s choice, and it is what makes
root finding, Laplace weights and the adjoint available. Masked discrete diffusion (D3PM, MDLM,
LLaDA) is better at language and has no continuous state, so no roots. A discrete implicit
learner, where a query’s answer is a fixed point of the denoiser’s categorical predictions, would
keep the relational interface with a discrete model. Lenticulum has nothing of the kind yet.
Joint answers or messages. token_marginals enumerates every answer, V^u of them for u
free positions. A language model needs the per-position beliefs passed between windows instead:
belief propagation on the chain, with categorical beliefs as messages. Pooling categorical beliefs
is exact and cheap (Categorical Belief),
but a window relation over continuous codes does not yet produce a categorical message for one
position given messages on the others.
Where long-range structure comes from. A chain of windows is Markov of order n-1. Longer
dependencies need wider windows (cost grows with nV) or latent variables: a summary of a
segment as its own variable, with relations between summaries. That is a factor graph with
latents, which Lenticulum’s design supports and nothing here builds yet.
Composition is not free for learned windows. The product of smoothed relations is not the
smoothed product, so composing networks is approximate at every noise level (Lenticulum’s
Language Models §7). On a chain of learned curves the smoothing bias adds up roughly linearly
in the length (product.md §4). How it behaves over hundreds of positions is open.
The moonshot. In the end, distil a small open-weight language model into such a graph:
relations between token sequences, with embeddings only at the input and output and per-position
categorical beliefs on the internal variables. Whether a pretrained model’s computation can be
dissected that way is the question this repository exists to answer.
4. The order of work
The roadmap, with the status of each step, is Open Problems in Assembling Language Models;
how the experiments, their data and the tools are set up is Environment and Experiments.
In short: learned windows on a character corpus (L2) come next, then messages instead of joint
answers (L5), then a discrete learner (L3) and scale (L4).
Related: tokens, sequence, Open Problems in Assembling Language Models, Map of Content

Design/Environment-and-Experiments.title: Environment and Experiments
Design/Environment-and-Experiments.content:
design

How the repository is meant to grow. LenticulumLM is a workspace for experiments, not a
library to install. A Nix flake sets up every tool they need, in shells. The Julia code in
src/ is the toolkit the experiments share, each experiment lives in its own directory with
its own environment, and large files (corpora, teacher models, checkpoints) live outside the
repository, pinned by a manifest and published to Hugging Face when they are worth sharing.
This note is the plan; only the flake and the toolkit exist so far.


Sources: original to this vault (design); code: flake.nix

1. What the flake does
flake.nix builds no package. It provides development shells, all with the same base:








































shelladdsfornix developJulia (the host’s, else the flake’s 1.12), git, git-lfs, jq, Node 22, Python with huggingface_hub (the hf CLI)the experiments, the docs and vault build, moving data and checkpointsnix develop .#gputhe host’s NVIDIA driver libraries, made visible to CUDA.jltraining on a GPU on a non-NixOS hostnix develop .#leanelanLean 4 and Mathlibnix develop .#metamathmetamathset.mm and its proofsnix develop .#isabelleIsabellethe Archive of Formal Proofsnix develop .#proversall three provers
Every shell sets LENTICULUMLM_ROOT, makes the repository the Julia project, and points
LENTICULUMLM_DATA and LENTICULUMLM_MODELS at ~/.cache/lenticulum/lm/{data,models}, next to
Lenticulum’s logs and models. Set them before entering to put the files elsewhere.
Some choices and their reasons:

The host’s Julia first. A julia already on the PATH (juliaup’s launcher, say) is used as
it is, so the shell adds nothing to a machine that has one; it warns below 1.11. Only without
one does the shell use the flake’s Julia (nix build .#julia), built on first entry. That is
nixpkgs’ 1.12 (julia_112-bin, 1.12.7) rather than its default 1.13: it is not in the binary
cache, and its build runs Julia’s whole test suite, more than twenty minutes, so the flake
switches the check off and the build takes ten seconds. Julia packages are pinned by each
project’s Manifest.toml through Pkg, not by Nix, and the shared ~/.julia depot serves
both Julias. A manifest resolved under one minor version needs Pkg.instantiate() under the
next, for its artifacts (the MNIST environment of Lenticulum, resolved under 1.12, misses
LLVMExtra’s 1.13 artifact).
elan, not a Lean toolchain: every Lean project pins its toolchain in a lean-toolchain
file, and elan fetches it; Mathlib’s compiled cache comes from lake exe cache get. Putting
a toolchain in Nix would pin it twice. The same holds for Mathlib.
The GPU shell links only the driver’s libraries (libcuda, libnvidia-*) into a private
directory. Putting the host’s /usr/lib on LD_LIBRARY_PATH would mix the host’s C library
into the shell. CUDA.jl brings its own CUDA toolkit as Julia artifacts; it needs only the
driver. It matters for the flake’s Julia, which does not search the host’s library paths:
with it, CUDA.jl is functional in .#gpu (RTX 3080) and not in the default shell. The host’s
own Julia finds the driver either way. On NixOS the driver is at /run/opengl-driver and
nothing is linked.

2. Layout as it grows








































wherewhattrackedsrc/, test/the shared toolkit (LenticulumLM) with its notes and testsyesexperiments/NN-name/one experiment: its own Project.toml (the toolkit by path, Lenticulum from GitHub), scripts, and a note NN-name.md with what was run and what came outyesexperiments/NN-name/Manifest.tomlthe exact package versions of a runyes, for experiments (see §5)data/manifest.tomlevery corpus, teacher model and checkpoint an experiment uses: where it comes from, its revision or hash, its licenceyes$LENTICULUMLM_DATA, $LENTICULUMLM_MODELSthe files themselvesnovault/design notes, the roadmap, and a note per experiment’s findingsyes
An experiment’s note follows the implementation-note practice: what it set out to measure,
what it measured, what did not work. Its numbers go into the vault when they change a
conclusion, as the MNIST notes do in Lenticulum.
3. Large files: data, teacher models, checkpoints
Pinned by a manifest, not by Nix. Corpora and models are gigabytes. Nix’s fixed-output
derivations would pin them by hash, but would also copy them into the store and keep them
there per version. Instead data/manifest.toml lists each file or repository with its source
and an exact revision:
[datasets.tinystories]
source = "hf:roneneldan/TinyStories"
revision = "<commit sha>"
licence = "CDLA-Sharing-1.0"
path = "tinystories"                     # under $LENTICULUMLM_DATA
A fetch script (Julia, or hf download --revision) reads it and fills $LENTICULUMLM_DATA;
a check verifies hashes. Small, stable inputs (a single set.mm, a word list) may still be
fixed-output derivations, where the store copy costs nothing.
Published to Hugging Face. Checkpoints worth keeping (.jld2 files of trained windows,
distilled relations) go to a Hugging Face repository under the MathStruct organisation, with a
model card that names the experiment, the commit of this repository that produced it, and the
data it saw. hf upload and hf download are in every shell; .jld2 is a binary file and is
stored with Git LFS on the Hugging Face side, never in this repository. Whether Julia’s JLD2 is
the right exchange format (versus safetensors, which Python tools read) is a decision to make
when the first checkpoint is published.
4. What is planned, and what each needs



































additionshelldataopen questionslearned windows on a character corpus (roadmap L2)default, gpua small text corpus (TinyStories, text8)the corpus and window size; the training budgeta teacher model to distil (roadmap L8)a Python shell (§5)a small open-weight model, e.g. a TinyStories model, Pythia-70M or SmolLM2-135M, or a small masked diffusion LMwhich teacher; what is distilled (logits, hidden states, or relations between positions)formal mathematics as a corpuslean, metamath, isabelleMathlib, set.mm, the Archive of Formal Proofswhether proofs are text to model or relations to learn (a proof step as a relation between goals)checkpoints on Hugging Facedefaultthe experiments’ outputsformat (§3), naming, licences of what they were trained on
5. Decisions still open

A Python shell for teacher models. Running a pretrained model means PyTorch and
transformers. In Nix that is python3Packages.torch (with CUDA, unfree and a long build)
or a uv-managed environment inside a shell, which is quicker but pinned by its own lock file
rather than by the flake. The likely split: Python extracts what the teacher computes
(logits, activations) into files; Julia trains the relations on them.
Experiment manifests. Lenticulum.jl ignores every Manifest.toml, which suits libraries.
An experiment’s result should be reproducible, so experiments are proposed to commit theirs.
The Lenticulum version. Project.toml takes Lenticulum from its master branch; an
experiment’s committed manifest pins the exact commit, which is enough. Pinning a tag in
[sources] becomes worth it once Lenticulum has releases.
macOS and CUDA. The shells are declared for aarch64-darwin too, without the GPU shell’s
driver handling; only x86_64-linux has been entered so far (Arch Linux, with and without a
host Julia).

Related: Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners,
Open Problems in Assembling Language Models, Start Here

Design/Open-Problems-in-Assembling-Langu.filePath: Design/Open Problems in Assembling Language Models.md
Design/Open-Problems-in-Assembling-Langu.title: Open Problems in Assembling Language Models
Design/Open-Problems-in-Assembling-Langu.content:
open-problem

The roadmap of LenticulumLM: every step from a closed-form n-gram chain to a language model
assembled from learned implicit relations, with its status and its evidence. One step is
done; the others are open, and some of them are open in Lenticulum as well.


Sources: original to this vault (analysis); code: tokens.jl, sequence.jl
Lenticulum (vault): Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning · Language Models · product

L1. A language model assembled from relations — done (closed form)
sequence_relation joins window relations with separators; with the closed-form windows of a
bigram chain, every query direction is answered to within 10^{-4} of the closed form, and every
completion is found (sequence §3). Without separators the error is 0.01 to 0.06 and grows
with the number of inner positions.
L2. Learned windows — open (next)
Train an energy network on the windows of a small corpus (characters of a text, V \approx 30,
n = 3 to 5), use it as the window relation, and measure the assembled model against the corpus’s
empirical n-gram statistics: per-query marginals, the smoothing bias, and how it adds up along
the sequence. The separators need the window’s marginal on the overlap, which is either a second
learned relation or the window queried with its other positions free.
L3. A discrete implicit learner — open
Masked discrete diffusion (D3PM, MDLM, LLaDA) models language better than continuous codes, but
has no continuous state to find roots in. A discrete learner would answer a query by a fixed
point of the denoiser’s per-position categorical predictions, with clamps on the known tokens.
What replaces the Jacobian, the Laplace weight and the adjoint there is open.
L4. Vocabulary scale — open
One-hot codes give a position V coordinates, so a query with u free positions has uV
unknowns. For a real vocabulary this needs low-dimensional learned embeddings (Diffusion-LM) with
a decoding step, or the discrete learner of L3.
L5. Messages instead of joint answers — open
token_marginals enumerates all V^u completions. Belief propagation on the chain of windows,
with categorical beliefs as messages, would cost O(L V^n) instead. It needs a window relation
to produce a categorical message for one position given categorical beliefs on the others, which
for continuous codes means integrating the relation over the codes of the other positions.
L6. Long-range structure — open
A chain of windows is Markov of order n - 1. Longer dependencies need latent variables (segment
summaries with relations between them) or other factor-graph structure than a chain. Which
structure a corpus supports, and how the latent relations are trained, is open.
L7. Composition of learned relations at t > 0 — open (shared with Lenticulum)
Products of smoothed relations are not smoothed products. On Lenticulum’s chain of learned curves
the bias grows about linearly in the number of relations (product.md §4) and shrinks at lower
noise levels. Over the length of a text this may dominate; correctors (MCMC at each level, as
in Du et al.) or lower levels are the known remedies.
L8. Distilling a pretrained model — moonshot
Dissect a small open-weight language model into a graph of language diffusion relations, with
embeddings only at the input and output. It depends on L3 to L6.
Summary


















































stepstatusL1assembly from relationsdone, closed form: exact in every query directionL2learned windowsopen, nextL3discrete implicit learneropenL4vocabulary scaleopenL5messages instead of joint answersopenL6long-range structureopenL7composition at t > 0open, shared with LenticulumL8distillationmoonshot
Related: Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners, sequence, tokens

Map-of-Content.title: Map of Content
Map-of-Content.content:
overview

Every note of the LenticulumLM vault, in reading order. How the vault is organised and what
its conventions are: Start Here. The implicit learners, products and beliefs this builds
on are explained in Lenticulum’s vault, and the
general category theory in the CT-ML wiki;
links to both are ordinary web links, links within this vault are wikilinks.

1. The idea

Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners: a language model whose parts are
relations over token positions, assembled by product; what is built, and the decisions ahead
README: the project pitch
Environment and Experiments: the Nix shells, the layout experiments will take, and where
data, teacher models and checkpoints live

1b. Background

Diffusion Language Models: the variants (continuous, uniform, masked, score-based, block) and
what each offers a relational model
How a Diffusion Language Model Generates: the sampler step by step; parallel decoding and its
price; conditioning as clamping
Meaning as a Relation over Text: meaning as a relation between texts and meanings; a
diffusion model as such a relation; composition by product
Embeddings in a Diffusion Language Model: why learned embeddings in the state collapse, why
drifting per-variable embeddings break a factor graph, and the embedding-free precedent
Factor Graphs against Mixtures of Experts and Agent Chains: points against beliefs; a mixture
of experts as a switch, a product as an overlay, an agent chain as point maps

2. Implementation

tokens: tokens as one-hot codes, one block of coordinates per position; queries as clamps
sequence: windows and separators assembled into one relation; an n-gram chain, exact in
every query direction

3. Verdict

Open Problems in Assembling Language Models: the roadmap, from the closed-form chain to
learned, scalable, long-range models

Orientation

Start Here: conventions
Bibliography: every cited work
Lenticulum’s Language Models
note: products of diffusion language models, and why the graph only pays off when it has structure

README.title: README
README.content:
LenticulumLM


A diffusion language model assembled from implicit learners. A language model is usually
one network that runs one way. LenticulumLM builds one from parts: each part is a relation
over a few token positions, the model is their product, and every query is answered by root
finding with the known tokens clamped. Continuation, backward prediction and infilling are the
same model asked with different clamps.
It builds on Lenticulum.jl, which provides the
implicit learners (diffusion models read as relations), their products, and their beliefs.

Status: research prototype. Julia, not registered, one author. What is here is exact
against closed forms; learned windows, a discrete learner and scale are open
(roadmap).

The idea
Text of L tokens over a vocabulary of V symbols is a point of \mathbb R^{VL}, one block
of coordinates per position, each token its one-hot code. A relation on a window of n
positions is an implicit learner on nV coordinates. Windows at every offset, joined by
separators on their overlaps,
p(x_1, \dots, x_L) = \frac{\prod_k p_{\mathrm{win}}(x_k, \dots, x_{k+n-1})}{\prod_k p_{\mathrm{sep}}(x_{k+1}, \dots, x_{k+n-1})},
are an n-gram model when the windows are its n-gram marginals, and a query clamps whatever
is known:

























queryclampedansweredcontinuationthe first tokensthe distribution of each later positionbackward predictionthe last tokensthe distribution of each earlier positioninfillingboth endsthe middle
Every answer of a query is a stable root of the model’s field, with a Laplace weight, and the
roots read per position are categorical beliefs.
A minimal example
using LenticulumLM
v = Vocabulary(['x', 'y'])
T = [0.9 0.1; 0.4 0.6]                     # a bigram chain, stationary π = (0.8, 0.2)
π₀ = [0.8, 0.2]
model, ps, st = sequence_relation(v, window_relation(v, π₀ .* T), window_relation(v, π₀), 3)
pos, P, _ = token_marginals(v, model, ps, st, ['x', nothing, 'y'])    # fill in the middle
P                                           # (0.6, 0.4) = T(x, ·) .* T(·, y), normalised
On a three-symbol chain, continuation, backward prediction and infilling all agree with the
closed form to 10^{-4}, with every completion found as its own answer
(src/sequence.md §3).
Layout
The repository mirrors Lenticulum.jl’s:

































wherewhatsrc/the package; an implementation note (.md) beside each .jl filetest/the test suite, against closed formsvault/the Obsidian vault: design, roadmap, bibliography (Start Here)docs/Documenter pages, Literate tutorials, and the Quartz build of the vault (docs/site/)flake.nixthe development shells: every tool the experiments needexperiments/one directory per experiment, each with its own environment (planned)
Setting up
LenticulumLM is a workspace for experiments rather than a library to install. The Nix flake
sets up everything: Julia (yours if it is on the PATH, else its own 1.12), the docs toolchain,
the Hugging Face CLI, and on request Lean, Metamath or Isabelle
(plan):
nix develop               # Julia, Node, Python with the hf CLI, git-lfs
nix develop .#gpu         # the same, with the host's NVIDIA driver visible to CUDA.jl
nix develop .#lean        # + elan; also .#metamath, .#isabelle, .#provers
Data and checkpoints live outside the repository, in $LENTICULUMLM_DATA and
$LENTICULUMLM_MODELS (default ~/.cache/lenticulum/lm/). With direnv, .envrc enters the
default shell on cd.
Without Nix
Neither LenticulumLM nor Lenticulum.jl is registered. Project.toml takes Lenticulum’s
packages from GitHub, so a clone instantiates on its own:
using Pkg
Pkg.activate("path/to/LenticulumLM")
Pkg.instantiate()
Pkg.test()
Developing against a local Lenticulum
To change both repositories at once, develop the local Lenticulum packages into the
environment. This overrides the GitHub sources in the (untracked) manifest:
Pkg.develop([PackageSpec(path = "../Lenticulum.jl"),
             PackageSpec(path = "../Lenticulum.jl/lib/LenticulumCore.jl"),
             PackageSpec(path = "../Lenticulum.jl/lib/Mycelium.jl"),
             PackageSpec(path = "../Lenticulum.jl/lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl")])
Reading the theory

The vault, on the web at mathstruct.org/LenticulumLM (the API
documentation is under api/dev), or in Obsidian:
open the repository root and start at vault/Start Here.md.
Lenticulum’s vault, for the implicit learners themselves:
mathstruct.org/Lenticulum.jl.
The CT-ML wiki, for the general category theory both build on:
mathstruct.org/CategoryTheory-ML-Wiki.

License
MIT, see LICENSE.

Start-Here.title: Start Here
Start-Here.content:
overview

How this vault is organised, the conventions every note follows, and how to read or extend
it. The notes themselves are indexed, in reading order, in Map of Content.

What lives where
The vault is the whole repository. Its notes sit beside what they describe:






























wherewhatexamplevault/concept and design notes, grouped by topicvault/Design/Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners.mdsrc/*.mdimplementation notes, one beside each Julia filesrc/sequence.md beside sequence.jlexperiments/*/one directory per experiment, with its own environment and a note on what it found (planned)meta/local working material, not part of the repository (ignored by git)
The tools come from the Nix flake (nix develop), and data and checkpoints live outside the
repository; both are planned in Environment and Experiments.
LenticulumLM builds on Lenticulum.jl, and its
vault builds on Lenticulum’s theory vault:
implicit learners, diffusion relations, products and separators, beliefs and factor graphs are
explained there and not repeated here. The general category theory both rest on lives in the
CT-ML wiki, the root vault. This vault keeps
only what is specific to language models: how text becomes a joint space, how a language model
is assembled from relations, and what does not work yet.
Conventions
Every note opens the same way:


a tag line: one or more of #definition, #theorem, #derivation, #algorithm,
#model, #design, #implementation, #comparison, #application, #open-problem,
#overview, #annotation, #example, #reference;


a summary in a blockquote: the claim of the note in two or three lines;


a sources block:

> Sources: the papers with exact definition and theorem numbers, then code: the
Julia files the note describes. A note that is our own analysis says so (“original to
this vault”).
> Lenticulum (vault): links to the Lenticulum notes the note builds on, and
> Theory (CT-ML wiki): links to the general concepts it uses. Both are ordinary web
links to the published pages, since they are other vaults.

Every cited work is collected in Bibliography, generated from docs/src/refs.bib;
new citations go into that file first. docs/site/link_sources.py then adds a
> Bibliography: line under each note’s sources, linking every recognised work to its entry.


Implementation notes additionally record, as carefully as what the file does, what it does
not do and the difficulties met on the way.
Mathematics is written in LaTeX ($…$, and $$ fences on their own lines); the website
renders it with KaTeX, and the build refuses notes whose display math would be truncated
(see docs/site/README.md). Commutative diagrams are ```tikz blocks, as in
Lenticulum’s vault.
Notation. A sequence of L tokens over a vocabulary of V symbols is a point
z \in \mathbb R^{VL}, one block of V coordinates per position (tokens). The joint-space
conventions are Lenticulum’s: inputs X are clamped, outputs Y solved for, latents U inferred,
z_0 is the evidence and \rho the per-coordinate precision.
Links between notes of this vault are [[wikilinks]] by note name.
Reading it

On the web: the vault is rendered with Quartz as the front page of
mathstruct.org/LenticulumLM; the API documentation is
under api/dev.
In Obsidian: open the repository root as a vault. The Inline TikZ community plugin
renders the diagrams.

Adding to it
If you implement something, put a markdown file next to the .jl file containing the
implementation, with the theory, the implementation, and an extensive description of the
implementation difficulties. A concept that is not specific to language models belongs in
Lenticulum’s vault (or, if it is general category theory, in the CT-ML wiki) first, and the note
here links to it.

index.title: LenticulumLM — theory vault
index.content:
LenticulumLM assembles a diffusion language
model from implicit learners: relations over a few token positions each, combined by product
into one model whose every query (continue, predict backwards, fill in) is root finding with the
known tokens clamped. It builds on Lenticulum.jl,
whose theory vault explains the implicit
learners themselves. This vault records what is specific to language: the design, the
implementation, and what does not work yet.
Where to start

Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners: the plan, and the decisions ahead
tokens and sequence: text as a joint space, and an n-gram chain assembled from
relations, exact in every query direction
Open Problems in Assembling Language Models: the roadmap, step by step

Everything else

Map of Content: every note, in reading order.
Start Here: how the vault is organised, its conventions, and how to read it in Obsidian.
README: the project pitch.
API documentation: the Julia package itself, built with Documenter.
Lenticulum’s vault and the
CT-ML wiki: the theory this builds on.

src/sequence.title: sequence
src/sequence.content:
implementation

A language model assembled from implicit learners: one relation per window of n
consecutive tokens, joined by separators on the overlaps. With the windows of an n-gram
chain this is that chain exactly, and one assembled relation answers continuation, backward
prediction and infilling, each to within 10^{-4} of the closed form.


Sources: code: sequence.jl, tokens.jl; Hinton, Training Products of Experts by Minimizing Contrastive Divergence, Neural Computation 2002 (the product); Du et al., Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: Compositional Generation using Energy-Based Diffusion Models and MCMC, ICML 2023 (adding scores, and why it is not exact at t > 0)
Bibliography: Hinton 2002
Lenticulum (vault): product §4 (separators, longer chains) · Implicit Diffusion Learners · Language Models §7

1. The construction
A window relation sees n consecutive positions. Applied at every offset and joined by a
separator on each overlap of two consecutive windows,
p(x_1, \dots, x_L) = \frac{\prod_{k=1}^{L-n+1} p_{\mathrm{win}}(x_k, \dots, x_{k+n-1})}{\prod_{k=2}^{L-n+1} p_{\mathrm{sep}}(x_k, \dots, x_{k+n-2})} .
When p_{\mathrm{win}} is the n-gram distribution of a stationary (n-1)-th order Markov chain
and p_{\mathrm{sep}} its (n-1)-gram marginal, this is the chain’s joint distribution: the
junction-tree factorisation of a path. sequence_relation builds it as a Lenticulum
ProductRelation, with the window relation on the coordinates of positions k, \dots, k+n-1
and the separator, weight -1, on the overlap. The same relation object and parameters are
used at every offset: the model is stationary, and its parameters are shared as a sliding
network’s would be.
window_relation(v, P) is the closed-form window: a Gaussian mixture of width s with one
component at the codes of every window (a_1, \dots, a_n) with P[a_1, \dots, a_n] > 0, weighted by
it. This is the relation a diffusion model trained on those windows would converge to, with
every derivative exact, so it is the test oracle for the assembly. A learned window would replace
it without changing anything else.
2. Reading the answers as tokens
A query clamps the known positions. implicit_mixture finds its stable roots, each with a
Laplace weight \propto e^{-U(z_k)}\det(\Sigma_k)^{1/2}, which is the probability of the completion
it represents. position_marginals decodes every root to its nearest codes and adds its weight
to the symbol it gives at each free position. The result is one categorical distribution per
free position, the marginal of the query’s posterior. token_marginals does both steps, and
position_beliefs turns the columns into LenticulumCore CategoricalBeliefs labelled with the
symbols, the belief type a factor graph over tokens passes along.
The number of roots is the number of completions with positive probability, V^u for u free
positions of a chain with full support. token_marginals starts 16 solves per completion by
default. That is fine for the test’s three symbols and hopeless for a real vocabulary (§4).
3. Measured
A stationary bigram chain over three symbols, T = \begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.3&0.1\\0.2&0.5&0.3\\0.3&0.2&0.5\end{pmatrix}, its
stationary \pi, window table \pi(a)T(a,b) and separator \pi. Width 0.05, the default nodes.
Errors are the largest difference of a marginal from its closed form:




































































Lqueryclosed formanswerserrorwithout separatorstime3[a, ?, ?], last position(T^2)_{a\cdot}92\cdot10^{-5}0.0138.7 s (first call, compiling)3[?, ?, c], first position\propto \pi(\cdot)(T^2)_{\cdot c}98\cdot10^{-5}0.0190.7 s3[a, ?, c]\propto T_{a\cdot}T_{\cdot c}31\cdot10^{-4}0.0420.2 s4[a, ?, ?, ?], last position(T^3)_{a\cdot}271\cdot10^{-5}0.0215.5 s4[?, ?, ?, c], first position\propto \pi(\cdot)(T^3)_{\cdot c}277\cdot10^{-5}0.0303.3 s4[a, ?, ?, c], position 2\propto T_{a\cdot}(T^2)_{\cdot c}99\cdot10^{-5}0.0601.1 s
Every completion is found, and every query direction is answered by the same relation. Without
the separators each inner position’s marginal counts once per window covering it, and the
error grows with the number of inner positions (Lenticulum’s product.md §4 measures the same for
chains of three to five binary relations).
4. What it does not do

The windows are not learned yet. window_relation is the exact relation of a known
table. A learned window (an energy network on nV coordinates, trained by denoising on the
windows of a corpus) plugs into sequence_relation unchanged. Training one, and measuring
how its smoothing bias adds up along a sequence, is the next step
(Open Problems in Assembling Language Models L2).
The separators are supplied. They must be the marginals of the windows on the overlaps,
or the product is not the chain. For a learned window that means a second learned relation,
or the window model queried with the other positions marginalised away.
Enumerating answers is exponential. A query with u free positions has up to V^u roots.
The categorical marginals here sum over all of them. A real model needs per-position beliefs
passed between windows (message passing on the chain) instead of the joint answers, which
means categorical beliefs over continuous codes (Open Problems in Assembling Language Models L5).
Composition is exact here only because the windows are closed form. For networks the
product of smoothed relations is not the smoothed product (the t > 0 obstruction of
Lenticulum’s Language Models §7), and the error is expected to add up along the chain like
the smoothing bias does.

Related: tokens, Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners,
Open Problems in Assembling Language Models

src/tokens.title: tokens
src/tokens.content:
implementation

Tokens as coordinates. A sequence of L tokens over V symbols is a point of
\mathbb R^{VL}: one block of V coordinates per position, each token its scaled one-hot code.
A query clamps the blocks of the known tokens and frees the rest, so the direction of a query
(continue, predict backwards, fill in) is a choice of precisions, not of model.


Sources: code: tokens.jl; Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation, NeurIPS 2022 (continuous codes for tokens); Austin et al., Structured Denoising Diffusion Models in Discrete State-Spaces, NeurIPS 2021 (the discrete alternative)
Bibliography: Li et al. 2022 · Austin et al. 2021
Lenticulum (vault): Implicit Diffusion Learners §2 (polarity is a precision vector) · MNIST in Both Directions (a label as a scaled one-hot code)

1. The encoding
Vocabulary(symbols; scale = C) numbers the symbols 1, \dots, V and gives symbol a the code
C e_a \in \mathbb R^V. Position i of a sequence owns the coordinates block(v, i)
= (i-1)V+1, \dots, iV, so a sequence is the concatenation of its codes:
z = (C e_{x_1}, \dots, C e_{x_L}) \in \mathbb R^{VL} .
decode reads each block back by its largest coordinate, which is the nearest code: the codes
are orthogonal and of equal length, so the nearest code to u is \arg\max_a u_a.
sequence_query(v, tokens) turns a partly known sequence (a symbol or nothing per position)
into the query of an implicit learner. The precision is \infty on the blocks of known tokens
(hard clamps) and 0 on the others (free), and z_0 holds the known codes. An unknown
position starts at zero, the centre of the codes, which favours no symbol.
This is the encoding of the MNIST example in Lenticulum, where the label is the code
C e_y \in \mathbb R^{10} next to the image. A language model has only labels.
2. What it does not do

It does not scale with the vocabulary. A block has V coordinates, so a sequence of L
tokens over a vocabulary of 5\cdot10^4 is a state of 5\cdot10^4 L coordinates, and every free
block of a query is V unknowns for the root finder. Diffusion-LM avoids this with learned
low-dimensional embeddings, and masked discrete diffusion (D3PM, MDLM) avoids it by not having
a continuous state at all. Both are open here
(Open Problems in Assembling Language Models L3, L4).
No tokeniser. Symbols are whatever the vocabulary is built from (characters, words,
integers). Splitting text into tokens is left to the caller.
No soft evidence. A query either clamps a position or frees it. A noisy observation of a
token would be a finite precision on its block, which the implicit learner supports but
sequence_query does not build yet.
The scale C matters, and is not chosen here. Relative to the noise levels of the learner,
C sets how far apart the codes are: too small and the answers of neighbouring symbols merge
under the smoothing, too large and the field is stiff. The default C = 1 with mixture width
0.05 separates them by 20 widths.

Related: sequence, Assembling a Language Model from Implicit Learners
